extracted.intended_audience: academics, grant reviewers, research policymakers, and scholars of peer review and higher-education evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and pragmatic rules used by peer-review panels to evaluate academic proposals and to organize deliberative review processes; includes disciplinary, procedural, and normative considerations that shape judgments of excellence and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence / Quality as moral and technical accomplishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Across fields, excellence is viewed as a moral as well as a technical accomplishment; it is thought to be a result of determination and hard work, humility, authenticity, and audacity. Other 'evanescent qualities' (e.g., elegance, display of cultural capital) also count, even when they run counter to meritocratic ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that panels treat excellence as multi-dimensional — both ethical/character traits and technical merit matter. Be aware that aesthetic/cultural signals (elegance, cultural capital) can influence judgments and may conflict with formal meritocratic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance is assessed in multiple ways: by the likely generalizability of findings; by how a topic informs our understanding of broader processes; or by the deeper understanding produced by a particular interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists should select the mode of 'significance' assessment appropriate to the discipline and project type; different proposals legitimately demand different standards of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disciplinary-appropriate standards while seeking cross-discipline consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators aim for consistency in standards across disciplines even as they use standards appropriate to the discipline of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance respecting disciplinary norms with a desire for comparable standards across panels. Expect negotiation and contextualization; do not impose a single universal metric uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinarity as part of excellence (but lacking agreed standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinarity and diversity are seen by many panelists as aspects of excellence, not alternatives. However, because there is little agreement about evaluation standards for interdisciplinary work, reviewers often fall back on existing disciplinary tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing interdisciplinary proposals, panels should be explicit about which disciplinary standards are being applied and be attentive to the risk of unfairly privileging conventional disciplinary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and legitimacy of the evaluative process
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists aim to 'produce the sacred' of fair evaluation: reciprocal recognition of authority, consensual and egalitarian decision making combined with deference to expertise, and a pragmatic conception of 'truth' as provisional and community-defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processes and customary rules that create a shared sense of justice are central to perceived legitimacy. Panels should cultivate reciprocal respect, transparent rules, and procedural rituals that sustain confidence in outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panelist self-concept and mutual evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists evaluate one another as they evaluate proposals; respect for customary rules sustains their identity as fair, expert academics. Panelists may downplay the influence of their self-concept even when it orients judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that social dynamics and reputational concerns shape how panelists argue and vote; selection and training should address these social-psychological forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of bias and homophily
rubrics_metrics.description: Biases are unavoidable (e.g., risk-avoidance, Matthew effect, preference for confirmatory work, gender/ideological bias). Homophily prevents identification of a wide range of talents and narrows selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educate panelists about homophily and other biases and foster active countermeasures (diverse panels, explicit criteria). Accept that subjectivity/intersubjectivity cannot be fully removed but can be mitigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies such as double-blinding are imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed remedies like double-blinding (or deleting bibliographic references that identify researchers) are suggested to overcome known pitfalls, but given the contextual and intersubjective nature of evaluation, these strategies will not eliminate bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat blinding and other technical fixes as potentially useful but limited tools; pair them with training, panel design changes, and reflexive practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel process design: size, order, rotation, selection, training, transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical questions about panel design matter: effective panel size, order in which panelists view proposal elements, frequency of rotating members, criteria (formal and informal) for choosing panelists, training of screeners, and advising/supervising program officers. Aim for greater transparency while preserving deliberation privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically evaluate and experiment with panel design choices (size, rotation, reading order). Provide structured training for screeners and program officers and publish process-level information to enhance accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and pragmatic constraints produce 'good enough' solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists must finish decision-making in the time allotted; they typically reach 'good enough' compromises rather than ideal solutions. Customary rules and pragmatic constraints shape behavior and justifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic expectations about what deliberation can achieve under time limits. Design procedures (agenda, time allocations) to reduce arbitrary outcomes and to focus discussion productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of excellence are socially embedded (role of networks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality and the identification of the 'cream' are produced through expert interaction and are rooted in networks of colleagues and ideas; proposals and people are socially embedded rather than naturally rising to the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and make explicit how networks and prior relationships influence judgments; seek mechanisms to surface and correct for network-driven advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performative effects of belief in meritocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in the legitimacy of a meritocratic system can create conditions that sustain it — the 'faith' in the system motivates care in evaluation and reinforces meritocratic practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster institutional narratives that balance critical reflection with belief in procedural fairness, since cynicism can reduce care in preparation and review of applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and cross-national conditions matter for exporting review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that facilitate U.S.-style peer review (large, dispersed university systems enabling blind review and centralized panels; conspicuous collegiality) do not necessarily exist elsewhere. Policymakers exporting the model must consider national institutional conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before adopting U.S. peer-review practices in other countries, empirically assess local conditions (size of academic community, geographic dispersion, role of unions and state, institutional legacies) and adapt processes accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of evaluative strategies and need for a general theory of valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals demand varied standards and a plurality of assessment strategies; to better understand valuation across domains we need a general theory that focuses on constraints and rules evaluators follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop conceptual frameworks and empirical studies to map the intersubjective conventions and pragmatic rules that legitimize different kinds of excellence across domains (journals, tenure, admissions, artistic and financial evaluations).
